items.section_title: 1.10 · Objective j — Arterial versus venous findings
items.html: Allen test. The patient clenches the fist for thirty seconds with both arteries occluded. The fist is then opened and one artery released to watch the hand fill.
cites: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 108

src.question: How long is the patient asked to clench the fist in the Allen test?
src.explanation: with both arteries occluded. The fist is then opened and one artery released to watch the hand fill.

items.section_title: 1.7 · Objective h — The physical characteristics of thrills and murmurs
items.html: Murmur timing with the carotid. A systolic murmur falls between S1 and S2 and a diastolic one between S2 and S1; systolic murmurs match the carotid upstroke, giving an external marker.
cites: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 50

src.question: How can palpating the carotid help with murmur timing?
src.key: Systolic murmurs match the carotid upstroke
src.explanation: Correct — a systolic murmur falls between S1 and S2, a diastolic one between S2 and S1, and the carotid gives you an external marker for which is which.

items.section_title: 1.9 · Objective i — Maneuvers to evaluate murmurs
items.html: Standing quickly from squatting. Blood pools in the legs and preload falls, so less blood returns to the heart; the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy murmur becomes louder and the aortic stenosis murmur softer.
cites: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 62

src.question: What happens when a patient stands quickly from squatting?
src.key: Blood pools in the legs; preload falls
src.explanation: Correct — less blood returns to the heart, so the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy murmur becomes louder and the aortic stenosis murmur softer.

items.section_title: 1.10 · Objective j — Arterial versus venous findings
items.html: Chronic venous insufficiency findings. Pain is usually none or mild, an ache or heaviness that eases with elevation. There is normal temperature and pitting edema, with hemosiderin staining, brown pigmentation, thickened skin, normal pulses, and gangrene rare or absent.
cites: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 93

src.question: What are the findings of chronic venous insufficiency?
src.key: Mild or no pain, normal temperature, pitting edema
src.explanation: Correct — pain is usually none or mild, an ache or heaviness that eases with elevation. Also hemosiderin staining with brown pigmentation, thickened skin, normal pulses, and gangrene rare or absent.

items.section_title: 1.8 · Objective h — The murmurs one by one
items.html: Pansystolic murmur. It begins with S1 and continues to S2, with something open through all of systole as blood flows from a high pressure chamber to a lower one through a structure that should be closed. All are pathologic.
cites: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 72

src.question: What defines a pansystolic murmur?
src.key: It begins with S1 and continues to S2
src.explanation: Correct — something is open through all of systole, with blood flowing from a high pressure chamber to a lower one through a structure that should be closed. All are pathologic.

items.section_title: 1.3 · Objective c — The cardiac cycle, heart sounds and gallops
items.html: Valves during ventricular systole. The pulmonic and aortic valves are open, while the tricuspid and mitral valves are closed; the right ventricle pumps into the pulmonary arteries and the left into the aorta.
cites: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 13

src.question: Which valves are open during ventricular systole?
src.explanation: Correct — the right ventricle pumps into the pulmonary arteries and the left into the aorta, while the tricuspid and mitral valves are closed.

items.section_title: 1.7 · Objective h — The physical characteristics of thrills and murmurs
items.html: Causes of a murmur. Ejection into a dilated chamber is a named cause, alongside flow across a partially obstructed valve, increased flow through a normal valve in a small child, regurgitant flow across an incompetent valve, and abnormal shunting to a lower pressure chamber.
cites: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 46

src.question: Which of these is a named cause of a murmur?
src.explanation: alongside flow across a partially obstructed valve, increased flow through a normal valve in a small child, regurgitant flow across an incompetent valve, and abnormal shunting to a lower pressure chamber.

items.section_title: 1.6 · Objective g — Using the diaphragm and the bell
items.html: Use of the diaphragm. The diaphragm is better for the high-pitched sounds, S1, S2 and rubs, and for the regurgitant murmurs too; it is pressed firmly and used to listen throughout the precordium.
cites: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 30

src.question: Which sounds is the diaphragm better for?
src.explanation: Correct — the high-pitched sounds. It is pressed firmly and used to listen throughout the precordium. The regurgitant murmurs too.

items.section_title: 1.8 · Objective h — The murmurs one by one
items.html: Mitral stenosis murmur. It is best heard with the bell at the apex, in the left lateral decubitus position: a low-pitched decrescendo rumble, mid to late diastolic, grade 1 to 4, with little or no radiation.
cites: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 79

src.question: How is the murmur of mitral stenosis best heard?
src.key: Bell at the apex, left lateral decubitus
src.explanation: Correct — a low-pitched decrescendo rumble, mid to late diastolic, grade 1 to 4, with little or no radiation.

items.section_title: 1.3 · Objective c — The cardiac cycle, heart sounds and gallops
items.html: S4 as a normal finding. S4 is considered normal in trained athletes and older populations; it is the mirror of S3, which is physiologic in the young and pathologic in the old, while S4 runs the other way.
cites: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 42

src.question: In whom is S4 considered normal?
src.explanation: which is the mirror of S3 — physiologic in the young and pathologic in the old, while S4 runs the other way.

items.section_title: 1.6 · Objective g — Using the diaphragm and the bell
items.html: Bell of the stethoscope. The bell is better for low-pitched sounds, such as S3, S4 and the murmur of mitral stenosis. It is applied lightly to the skin, ensuring no gaps, at the apex and moving medially along the lower sternal border.
cites: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 30

src.question: Which sounds is the bell better for?
src.explanation: Correct — S3, S4 and the murmur of mitral stenosis. It is applied lightly to the skin, ensuring no gaps, at the apex and moving medially along the lower sternal border.

items.section_title: 1.3 · Objective c — The cardiac cycle, heart sounds and gallops
items.html: Mid-systolic murmur with physiologic splitting of S2. The murmur sits in the middle of systole and the split of S2 comes and goes with breathing, which is physiologic.
cites: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 35

src.question: Heard at the pulmonic area with the patient supine, over several breaths. What is this murmur?
src.key: Mid-systolic murmur with physiologic splitting of S2
src.explanation: Correct. The murmur sits in the middle of systole and the split of S2 comes and goes with breathing, which is physiologic.

items.section_title: 1.3 · Objective c — The cardiac cycle, heart sounds and gallops
items.html: Mid-systolic murmur with pathologic splitting of S2. The murmur sits in the middle of systole and the split of S2 stays audible during expiration, which is pathologic and suggests heart disease.
cites: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 35

src.question: Heard at the pulmonic area with the patient supine, over several breaths. What is this murmur?
src.key: Mid-systolic murmur with pathologic splitting of S2
src.explanation: Correct. The murmur sits in the middle of systole and the split of S2 stays audible during expiration, which is pathologic and suggests heart disease.

items.section_title: 1.3 · Objective c — The cardiac cycle, heart sounds and gallops
items.html: S3 gallop with a holosystolic murmur. An S3 after S2 (Ken-TUC-ky) with a murmur that fills systole fits volume overload from mitral regurgitation, which causes both.
cites: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 40

src.question: Heard at the apex with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position. What is this murmur?
src.key: S3 gallop with a holosystolic murmur
src.explanation: Correct. An S3 after S2 (Ken-TUC-ky) with a murmur that fills systole fits volume overload from mitral regurgitation, which causes both.

items.section_title: 1.3 · Objective c — The cardiac cycle, heart sounds and gallops
items.html: Ejection sound with a mid-systolic murmur. An ejection sound comes right after S1 and is high pitched; with a midsystolic murmur at the pulmonic area it fits pulmonic stenosis, which causes both.
cites: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 38

src.question: Heard at the pulmonic area with the patient supine, over several breaths. What is this murmur?
src.key: Ejection sound with a mid-systolic murmur
src.explanation: Correct. An ejection sound comes right after S1 and is high pitched; with a midsystolic murmur at the pulmonic area it fits pulmonic stenosis, which causes both.

items.section_title: 1.3 · Objective c — The cardiac cycle, heart sounds and gallops
items.html: Opening snap, then a diastolic murmur. The snap of a stenotic mitral valve opening is followed by the low-pitched mid to late diastolic murmur of mitral stenosis, heard with the bell at the apex.
cites: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 44

src.question: Heard at the apex with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position. What is this murmur?
src.key: Opening snap, then a diastolic murmur
src.explanation: Correct. The snap of a stenotic mitral valve opening is followed by the low-pitched mid to late diastolic murmur of mitral stenosis, heard with the bell at the apex.

items.section_title: 1.3 · Objective c — The cardiac cycle, heart sounds and gallops
items.html: S4 gallop with a mid-systolic murmur. The dull S4 just before S1 (Ten-nes-SEE) is followed by a murmur in the middle of systole; aortic stenosis and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy are causes of both.
cites: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 42

src.question: Heard at the apex with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position. What is this murmur?
src.key: S4 gallop with a mid-systolic murmur
src.explanation: Correct. The dull S4 just before S1 (Ten-nes-SEE) is followed by a murmur in the middle of systole; aortic stenosis and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy are causes of both.

items.section_title: 1.8 · Objective h — The murmurs one by one
items.html: Pulmonic stenosis radiation. The murmur radiates toward the left shoulder and neck, if loud, from the pulmonic area. It is midsystolic, crescendo-decrescendo, medium and harsh, and no maneuvers are listed for it.
cites: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 68

src.question: Where does the murmur of pulmonic stenosis radiate?
src.key: Toward the left shoulder and neck, if loud
src.explanation: Correct, from the pulmonic area. It is midsystolic, crescendo-decrescendo, medium and harsh, and no maneuvers are listed for it.

items.section_title: 2.5 · Objective e — Crackles, wheezes and rhonchi compared
items.html: Where to hear the mediastinal crunch. The mediastinal crunch (Hamman sign), precordial crackles in time with the heartbeat, is best heard with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position.
cites: 6. Thorax - Dr. Crowe.pptx, Slide 51

src.question: In which position is the mediastinal crunch (Hamman sign) best heard?
src.explanation: Correct: the mediastinal crunch, precordial crackles in time with the heartbeat, is best heard with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position.

items.section_title: 2.2 · Objective b — The respiratory history
items.html: Grading how severe dyspnea is. Functional severity is graded by walking distance, how many flights of stairs the patient can climb without stopping, everyday tasks and change from baseline.
cites: 6. Thorax - Dr. Crowe.pptx, Slide 12

src.question: Which question assesses the functional severity of dyspnea?
src.key: How many flights of stairs can you climb?
src.explanation: Correct: functional severity is graded by walking distance, flights of stairs without stopping, everyday tasks and change from baseline.

items.section_title: 2.5 · Objective e — Crackles, wheezes and rhonchi compared
items.html: Coarse against fine crackles. Coarse crackles are louder, lower in pitch, start early in inspiration and last through expiration, and do not change with body position (larger airway secretions or fluid); fine crackles change with body position.
cites: 6. Thorax - Dr. Crowe.pptx, Slide 47

src.question: How do coarse crackles differ from fine crackles?
src.key: They do not change with body position
src.explanation: Correct: coarse crackles are louder, lower in pitch, start early in inspiration and last through expiration, and do not change with position (larger airway secretions or fluid).

items.section_title: 3.2 · Objective a — The hematologic history
items.html: Family history of hemolysis. The family history asks about anemia, hemoglobinopathy, abnormal bleeding and unexplained jaundice, and relatives requiring transfusions or splenectomy, which raises suspicion for an inherited hemolytic disorder.
cites: Anemia-PDII-Ward-STUDENT-COPY-Updated.pptx, Slide 13

src.question: Which family history finding raises suspicion for an inherited hemolytic disorder?
src.explanation: Correct. The family history asks about anemia, hemoglobinopathy, abnormal bleeding and unexplained jaundice, and relatives requiring transfusions or splenectomy.

items.section_title: 3.5 · Objective d — Severity and specificity
items.html: Severe anemia. Symptoms at rest, chest pain and syncope are the severity markers; patients with them need urgent assessment. Fatigue and weakness are common even in mild anemia.
cites: Anemia-PDII-Ward-STUDENT-COPY-Updated.pptx, Slides 8, 54

src.question: Which symptom in an anemic patient most strongly suggests SEVERE anemia?
src.explanation: Correct. Symptoms at rest, chest pain and syncope are the severity markers; patients with them need urgent assessment. Fatigue and weakness are common even in mild anemia.

items.section_title: 1.4 · Objectives d & e — The apical impulse and point of maximal impulse
items.html: Pulse amplitude scale. 4 plus is bounding, 3 plus increased, 2 plus brisk and normal, 1 plus faint or diminished and 0 absent; always compare both sides.
cites: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 86

src.question: What does an amplitude of 2 plus indicate?
src.explanation: Correct, on a scale where 4 plus is bounding, 3 plus increased, 1 plus faint or diminished and 0 absent. The standing instruction is to always compare both sides.

items.section_title: 2.3 · Objective c — Disease processes associated with clubbing and hemoptysis
items.html: Clubbing and the lung. Clubbing is seen in interstitial lung disease and pulmonary fibrosis, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, lung abscess, lung cancer and congenital heart disease.
cites: 6. Thorax - Dr. Crowe.pptx, Slides 26, 33

src.question: Clubbing is associated with which lung condition?
src.explanation: Correct: clubbing is seen in interstitial lung disease and pulmonary fibrosis, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, lung abscess, lung cancer and congenital heart disease.

items.section_title: 3.2 · Objective a — The hematologic history
items.html: Gastrointestinal history and malabsorption. Celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, chronic diarrhea and gastrointestinal surgery are on the history because they impair absorption of iron or B12 and can cause anemia.
cites: Anemia-PDII-Ward-STUDENT-COPY-Updated.pptx, Slides 14, 10

src.question: Which gastrointestinal history is asked about because it can cause anemia through malabsorption?
src.explanation: Correct. Celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, chronic diarrhea and gastrointestinal surgery are on the history because they impair absorption of iron or B12.

items.section_title: 2.5 · Objective e — Crackles, wheezes and rhonchi compared
items.html: Mediastinal crunch history. The crunch is associated with tracheobronchial injury, blunt trauma, pulmonary edema, recreational drugs, childbirth and rapid ascent from scuba diving.
cites: 6. Thorax - Dr. Crowe.pptx, Slide 51

src.question: Which history is associated with a mediastinal crunch?
src.explanation: Correct: the crunch is associated with tracheobronchial injury, blunt trauma, pulmonary edema, recreational drugs, childbirth and rapid ascent from scuba diving.

items.section_title: 1.2 · Objective b — The cardiac history
items.html: Syncope. Syncope is transient loss of consciousness followed by recovery; the most common cause is neurocardiogenic, also called vasovagal, with a cardiac origin from arrhythmias in about 20 percent of cases.
cites: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 9

src.question: What is the most common cause of syncope?
src.explanation: Correct, with a cardiac origin from arrhythmias in about 20 percent of cases. Syncope itself is transient loss of consciousness followed by recovery.

items.section_title: 2.5 · Objective e — Crackles, wheezes and rhonchi compared
items.html: Fine crackles. Fine crackles are soft, higher pitched and very brief, heard mid to late inspiration, especially in dependent lung, and change with body position.
cites: 6. Thorax - Dr. Crowe.pptx, Slide 47

src.question: Which description fits FINE crackles?
src.explanation: Correct: fine crackles are softer, higher pitched and very brief, heard mid to late inspiration, especially in dependent lung, and change with body position.

items.section_title: 1.3 · Objective c — The cardiac cycle, heart sounds and gallops
items.html: The first heart sound. S1 is produced by closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves: as the ventricles contract, ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure, blood pushes the leaflets closed and the papillary muscles contract to assist.
cites: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 13

src.question: What produces the first heart sound?
src.key: Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves
src.explanation: Correct. As the ventricles contract, ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure, blood pushes the leaflets closed and the papillary muscles contract to assist.

items.section_title: 1.8 · Objective h — The murmurs one by one
items.html: Aortic stenosis murmur. Midsystolic, crescendo-decrescendo and harsh, with medium pitch, in the aortic area, radiating often to the carotids, down the left sternal border and even to the apex; a thrill implies grade 4 or above.
cites: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 67

src.question: Describe the murmur of aortic stenosis.
src.explanation: Correct, in the aortic area, radiating often to the carotids, down the left sternal border and even to the apex. A thrill implies grade 4 or above. The pitch is medium.

items.section_title: 1.3 · Objective c — The cardiac cycle, heart sounds and gallops
items.html: Physiologic S3. Expected in children and young adults to about 35 or 40, and in the last trimester of pregnancy; in adults over 40 the same sound is pathologic.
cites: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 40

src.question: In whom is a physiologic S3 expected?
src.key: Children and young adults to about 35 or 40
src.explanation: Correct, and in the last trimester of pregnancy. In adults over 40 the same sound is pathologic.

items.section_title: 1.9 · Objective i — Maneuvers to evaluate murmurs
items.html: Aortic stenosis and maneuvers. The aortic stenosis murmur is better sitting forward and louder on squatting: squatting and leg raise increase venous return and preload, sending more blood past the narrowed valve.
cites: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 67

src.question: Which maneuvers affect the murmur of aortic stenosis?
src.key: Better sitting forward; louder on squatting
src.explanation: Correct, because both squatting and leg raise increase venous return and preload, sending more blood past the narrowed valve. Leg raise does the same.

items.section_title: 1.10 · Objective j — Arterial versus venous findings
items.html: Edema and surface anatomy. Edema obscures veins, tendons and bones, which is why inspection notes relative size, symmetry and the prominence of those structures, and why one limb is always compared with the other.
cites: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 87

src.question: What does edema do to the surface anatomy of a limb?
src.key: It obscures veins, tendons and bones
src.explanation: Correct, which is why inspection notes relative size, symmetry and the prominence of those structures — and why one limb is always compared with the other.

items.section_title: 1.3 · Objective c — The cardiac cycle, heart sounds and gallops
items.html: Physiologic splitting of S2. Normal physiologic splitting of S2 is best heard in the pulmonic area, and can also be heard at Erb's point; its intensity increases with inspiration.
cites: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 34

src.question: Where is normal physiologic splitting of S2 best heard?
src.explanation: Correct, and splitting can also be heard at Erb's point. Its intensity increases with inspiration, and S2 follows the carotid pulse.

items.section_title: 3.2 · Objective a — The hematologic history
items.html: Surgical history. Gastric bypass, gastrectomy and intestinal resection are listed risks for iron or B12 deficiency: they impair absorption, so a patient can be deficient despite a good diet.
cites: Anemia-PDII-Ward-STUDENT-COPY-Updated.pptx, Slide 10

src.question: Which surgical history is a risk factor for iron or B12 deficiency?
src.explanation: Correct. Gastric bypass, gastrectomy and intestinal resection are listed risks: they impair absorption, so a patient can be deficient despite a good diet.

items.section_title: 1.4 · Objectives d & e — The apical impulse and point of maximal impulse
items.html: Right ventricular pressure overload. Pulmonic stenosis and pulmonary hypertension cause a right ventricular pressure overload impulse, a more forceful tapping with a sustained duration, the right-sided mirror of aortic stenosis and hypertension on the left.
cites: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 24

src.question: Which conditions cause a right ventricular pressure overload impulse?
src.explanation: Correct, producing a more forceful tapping with a sustained duration — the right-sided mirror of aortic stenosis and hypertension on the left.

items.section_title: 1.3 · Objective c — The cardiac cycle, heart sounds and gallops
items.html: Opening snap. Best heard just medial to the apex and at the lower sternal border; if loud enough it may radiate to the apex and to the pulmonic area.
cites: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 44

src.question: Where is an opening snap best heard?
src.key: Just medial to the apex, and the lower sternal border
src.explanation: Correct, and if loud enough it may radiate to the apex and to the pulmonic area.

items.section_title: 3.1 · Objective a — The three causes of anemia and the thresholds
items.html: Three mechanisms of anemia. Anemia comes from blood loss (bleeding), destruction (hemolysis) or impaired production; sorting a patient into one of these three is what the history and examination are for.
cites: Anemia-PDII-Ward-STUDENT-COPY-Updated.pptx, Slide 3

src.question: Which three mechanisms account for anemia?
src.key: Blood loss, destruction and impaired production
src.explanation: Correct. Anemia comes from red cells being lost (bleeding), destroyed (hemolysis) or not made (impaired production). Sorting a patient into one of these three is what the history and examination are for.

items.section_title: 2.6 · Objective f — Asthma, atelectasis, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pleural effusion compared
items.html: Pneumonia likelihood. In a patient with fever and cough, bronchial breath sounds plus egophony more than triples the likelihood of pneumonia.
cites: 6. Thorax - Dr. Crowe.pptx, Slide 54

src.question: In a patient with fever and cough, which pair of findings more than triples the likelihood of pneumonia?
src.explanation: Correct: with fever and cough, bronchial breath sounds plus egophony more than triples the likelihood of pneumonia.

items.section_title: 3.4 · Objective c — Signs and symptoms from other organ systems
items.html: B12 neurologic findings without anemia. Neurologic findings of B12 deficiency can occur without anemia or macrocytosis, so a normal blood count does not rule out the deficiency in a patient with these findings.
cites: Anemia-PDII-Ward-STUDENT-COPY-Updated.pptx, Slide 50

src.question: Can the neurologic findings of B12 deficiency occur without anemia?
src.explanation: Correct. Neurologic findings of B12 deficiency can occur without anemia or macrocytosis, so a normal blood count does not rule out the deficiency in a patient with these findings.

items.section_title: 1.8 · Objective h — The murmurs one by one
items.html: Mitral regurgitation murmur. Pansystolic at the apex and harsh, with medium to high frequency, radiating to the left axilla, with an apical thrill if loud; the harshness is attributed to the left ventricle being the powerful chamber.
cites: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 74

src.question: Describe the murmur of mitral regurgitation.
src.explanation: Correct, radiating to the left axilla, with an apical thrill if loud. The harshness is attributed to the left ventricle being the powerful chamber. The frequency is medium to high.
